data.title: State
data.tagline: State is information the interface needs to remember right now and that can change from actions or results.
data.learningOutcome: You can identify which state changes across an action and ask for accurate pending, success, and error feedback.
data.description: A form submitting, a modal being open, a cart count, and the active filter are all state. A component shows different output from those values. State is not the component itself, and not every long-lived record belongs only in page state.

learning.assumes: You have used a modal that opens and closes or seen a button change from Submit to Saving.
learning.outcome: You can identify which state changes across an action and ask for accurate pending, success, and error feedback.

distinctions.label: Component
distinctions.explanation: State records a current value or phase. A Component reads that state and renders the matching interface.

explanation.title: Remember the current condition
explanation.text: After Save is clicked, the page records that it is submitting, preventing repeat clicks and showing progress; it then changes to success or error when the request ends.

explanation.title: State drives what appears
explanation.text: The same button and message area show different content for different values. A state change should come from an actual action or request result, not an early success label.

explanation.title: What state looks like in code
explanation.text: In React, useState is the most common way to declare state. For example, useState(false) creates a state that starts as false. When the user clicks, the code calls the setter function to change the value, and React automatically updates the UI to match. When AI says “add a loading state”, it usually means creating a boolean state variable to toggle a spinner.

data.boundary: State is neither a component nor automatically a database. A component marks an interface responsibility; a database holds information that must persist across devices or users. Temporary page state disappearing on refresh cannot prove a server saved anything.

lessonPractice.title: A page shows “Saved” immediately after a click, but the network request then fails. What change fits best?

options.label: Enter a Saving state first, show Saved only after success, and show a retryable error on failure
options.feedback: Correct. Pending, success, and failure are different states, and the interface should change from the actual request result.

options.label: Keep showing Saved immediately because users dislike waiting
options.feedback: That treats interface text as proof and makes users think data was stored when it was not.

options.label: Remove every status message so no error text appears
options.feedback: People still need to know whether an action is pending, succeeded, or failed. Removing feedback does not make state accurate.

data.agentPrompt: Check the state in this save flow: after a click, show Saving and prevent duplicate submission; show Saved only after the API succeeds; show an error and retry path on failure. Verify both success and failure afterward.
